title: Watching our cosmic neighborhood
caption: The Milky Way and the Magellanic Clouds above three Auxiliary Telescopes, Paranal Observatory, Chile
celestial: Photograph taken at Paranal Observatory, Chile

recognition.text: ESO Picture of the Week (an editorial selection, not an audience score).

story: Three of the Auxiliary Telescopes at ESO’s Paranal Observatory stand beneath the band of the Milky Way and both Magellanic Clouds in this view from Chile’s Atacama Desert. The sky here is so dark that all of these can be seen with the unaided eye.

The Large and Small Magellanic Clouds are irregular dwarf galaxies held by our galaxy’s gravity, about 160,000 and 200,000 light-years away. In this photograph, the Small Magellanic Cloud and the lower Milky Way are bathed in a green glow called airglow, very faint light given off by oxygen atoms high in the atmosphere.

Four of these 1.8-meter telescopes feed light into the Very Large Telescope Interferometer, and each can roll along tracks to any of 30 observing stations. Working together, they act like one “virtual” telescope as big as the distance between them. Among their feats: the first close-up image of a star outside our galaxy, WOH G64, a red supergiant in the Large Magellanic Cloud.

understand.summary: A ground-based landscape photograph credited to ESO/N. Schafer. The source does not publish camera, exposure or color-processing details.
understand.eye: A camera can gather light for longer than the eye, so the Milky Way looks brighter and more detailed here than it would to someone standing on site.

explore: Changing the spacing between the Auxiliary Telescopes changes how much detail the combined instrument can see, a little like adjusting the size of one enormous mirror.
alt: Three small dome-shaped telescopes on a desert platform beneath the Milky Way, with two hazy patches of light, the Magellanic Clouds, and a green glow low in the sky.
